<reason>Both sides built coherent, competitive cases, but A maintained a sharper comparative frame throughout: a concrete, named cost (a flagged individual released when a detainer is declined) versus a diffuse, unproven trust benefit. A's pressure question on evidence for policy-label-specific reporting effects landed hardest, and B's answer (A1 in Rebuttal 2) reasserted the mechanism narrative rather than directly engaging the evidentiary gap—an execution cost under the "dodge" penalty. A also introduced a clever population distinction (victims/witnesses vs. jail-booked detainees) that meaningfully complicated B's "one hold teaches the whole block" story; B's closing attempt to re-merge these populations was asserted rather than established. B's domestic-violence framing and "predators lose easy prey" narrative were vivid and never fully dismantled, and B's answer on ICE's residual tools (administrative warrants, own-authority arrests) added real substance in Rebuttal 2. But on balance A's closing weighing ("a name and a file" vs. "a theory about rumor") crystallized the clash more cleanly and left B's rebuttal to the population split as the least resolved thread at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1) distinguishing victims/witnesses from jail-booked detainees, directly answering B's pressure question while undercutting B's core "whole block learns not to call" mechanism—only partially countered in B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
